newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair, Major row as EU's Santer weighs in.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair, Major row as EU's Santer weighs in.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major and opposition Labour leader Tony Blair, facing a general election on May 1, traded jibes on Tuesday over who would best defend Britain in Europe after a surprise intervention by EU Commission president Jacques Santer.
Santer, head of the 15-nation EU's executive body, on Monday made a spirited attack on Eurosceptic "doom merchants" and insisted that European states should move towards closer integration.
Major seized on Santer's remarks, telling a news conference he had warned that Britain would face strong pressures to agree to integrationist moves at the European Union summit in Amsterdam in June.

"Yesterday, President Santer confirmed these are exactly the things that others in Europe want to secure and Mr Blair made a speech in which he made clear that many of these objectives are objectives Labour share..."

"I will keep returning to the point that it is only a Conservative government that can be trusted to say 'no' to a federal Europe... There is now a sharp dividing line between the parties on Europe," Major said.

Blair hit back, saying it was Major who had Santer appointed after arguing he would be less federalist than Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, original favourite for the job when France's Jacques Delors resigned.
But Labour's leader was clearly unhappy about Santer's intervention, which the party's home affairs spokesman Jack Straw described earlier as "ill-judged and unwise".
He dismissed suggestions the speech could damage Labour's campaign, saying: "What Mr Santer says, with all due respect, is neither here nor there. I disagree with a lot of what he said.
"Mr Santer represents the European Commission, if I am elected I will represent Britain."

The Conservatives, way behind in opinion polls, are riven with dissent over Europe's planned single currency, with over 200 candidates and even some ministers saying they would vote against Britain joining in defiance of the official "wait-and-see" policy.
But Conservative strategists saw Santer's speech as a chance to unite the fractious ruling party against a foreign enemy.

Even the minority Liberal Democrats, who expect to win around a dozen seats on May 1 and who want closer European links, were upset by Santer's comments. Party leader Paddy Ashdown said: "I'm not in favour of a European superstate."
The row over Europe, which has now dominated campaigning for a week, drowned out other issues designed to be the focus of campaigning on Tuesday.
The Conservatives unveiled proposals to cut crime by 10 percent and put more police on the streets, while Labour announced plans to boost Britain's economic competitiveness.
